what: Apple Hospitality REIT owns about 220 upscale select-service hotels across the US, mostly under Marriott and Hilton brands such as Courtyard, Residence Inn, Hampton Inn and Homewood Suites. It owns the properties and hires third-party managers to run them.
customers: Business and leisure travellers staying in mid-priced hotels in suburban and secondary markets.
money: Nightly room rates at its hotels.
moat: A diversified, low-debt portfolio of efficient select-service hotels with strong brands behind them. Select-service hotels need fewer staff than full-service ones, so margins hold up better.
risks: Hotel demand is cyclical and falls quickly in a slowdown.
Revenue per available room has flattened: revenue fell from $1.43B in 2024 to $1.41B in 2025.
Rising labour, insurance and property tax costs squeeze margins.
The P/E is not useful for a REIT; funds from operations matter.
opportunities: Debt of $1.5B against $3.2B of equity is conservative for a hotel REIT.
The dividend yields about 5%, paid monthly.
Free cash flow of about $300M a year comfortably covers the dividend.
Share buybacks when the stock is cheap.
watch: Revenue per available room and hotel operating margins.
view: Apple Hospitality is a conservative hotel REIT: low debt, select-service hotels with strong brands, and a monthly dividend of about 5% that free cash flow covers comfortably. The P/E of 25 is not the right measure for a REIT; on cash flow the shares trade at about 15 times.

The challenge is growth. Hotel revenue has flattened as travel demand cooled after the post-pandemic rebound, and costs keep rising. The market is pricing it as a steady income stock with little growth, which seems fair.

This turns on room rates and occupancy. If they hold, the dividend is safe and buybacks add a little each year; if a slowdown hits travel, the low debt gives it room to keep paying. I would call it fairly priced for income rather than a bargain.
bull: Travel demand picks up and higher room rates lift margins.
bear: A slowdown hits hotel demand while costs keep rising.
